Ethics in psychology. The field of moral and professional standards governing research on human and animal subjects, including requirements for informed consent, protection from harm, confidentiality, and institutional oversight. The field emerged from landmark violations that exposed the psychological damage researchers could inflict and prompted the development of ethics boards and formal research protocols.

Early psychology lacked ethical safeguards. Researchers conducted experiments on vulnerable populations—infants, prisoners, and psychiatric patients—without informed consent or regard for psychological harm. The Little Albert experiment in nineteen twenty traumatized an eleven-month-old by conditioning a fear of white rats. Albert suffered lasting phobia and was never desensitized, highlighting the failure to protect research subjects. Stanley Milgram's obedience experiments, conducted from nineteen sixty-one to nineteen sixty-two, led participants to believe they were delivering lethal electric shocks. Participants experienced severe psychological distress, and many emerged believing they had harmed another human. The Stanford Prison Experiment in nineteen seventy-one induced psychological breakdown in student participants randomly assigned to guard and prisoner roles. The study was halted early because conditions became abusive and dehumanizing.

The Nuremberg Code, developed in nineteen forty-seven after Nazi medical atrocities, first established the principle of informed consent. Psychology adopted similar standards through the American Psychological Association's ethics code. Modern institutional review boards, or IRBs, now require risk-benefit analysis, informed consent, confidentiality protections, and the right to withdraw. Violations can result in funding loss and professional sanctions. Ongoing debates remain about whether certain landmark studies could ever be approved today, and whether the knowledge gained about human obedience and conformity justifies the psychological harm inflicted on participants.
